summary: Psalm 15 opens with a question about who may dwell in Yahweh’s sanctuary and live on his holy hill. The answer is a compact portrait of a person whose conduct is truthful, loyal, just, and resistant to exploitation. The psalm closes by saying that the one who does these things “shall never be shaken.”
whyItMatters: This psalm stands in Book I of Psalms as a brief wisdom-like orientation to life before God. It links worship near the sanctuary with ordinary speech, money, promises, and treatment of neighbors.

context.author: The heading says, “A Psalm by David.” Psalms as a book is a many-voiced anthology, and Davidic headings may indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging; their precise historical force is debated.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that received the Psalms for public prayer and private life.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; assigning one date to the whole Psalter would be misleading.
context.setting: The psalm is oriented toward Yahweh’s sanctuary and holy hill, language that fits Psalms’ frequent orientation toward Jerusalem and temple worship, while the exact occasion is not identified.
context.literaryForm: A short Hebrew poem within the Psalter, framed as a question and answer about the kind of life fitting for dwelling near God.

outline.heading: The Entrance Question
outline.note: The speaker asks who may dwell in Yahweh’s sanctuary and live on his holy hill.

outline.heading: Integrity and Truth
outline.note: The answer begins with blameless conduct, doing what is right, and truthful inward speech.

outline.heading: Neighbor-Protecting Speech
outline.note: The description turns to what the person refuses to do: slander, harm a friend, or cast slurs.

outline.heading: Loyalties and Costly Promises
outline.note: The person rejects what is vile, honors those who fear Yahweh, and keeps an oath even when it hurts.

outline.heading: Justice With Money
outline.note: The final traits concern refusing usury and bribes, followed by the promise that such a person shall never be shaken.

keyVerses.text: A Psalm by David. Yahweh, who shall dwell in your sanctuary? Who shall live on your holy hill?
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the psalm its governing question: what kind of person may live near Yahweh’s holy presence?

keyVerses.text: He who walks blamelessly and does what is right, and speaks truth in his heart;
keyVerses.why: This verse begins the answer by joining outward conduct with inward truthfulness.

keyVerses.text: in whose eyes a vile man is despised, but who honors those who fear Yahweh; he who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change;
keyVerses.why: This verse shows that the psalm’s portrait includes moral judgment, reverence for Yahweh, and costly reliability.

keyVerses.text: he who doesn’t lend out his money for usury, nor take a bribe against the innocent. He who does these things shall never be shaken.
keyVerses.why: This verse completes the portrait with economic justice and gives the psalm’s closing assurance.

questions.question: What is the main question of Psalm 15?
questions.answer: The psalm asks who may dwell in Yahweh’s sanctuary and live on his holy hill. The rest of the poem answers by describing a person’s conduct, speech, loyalties, promises, and use of money. The chapter does not give a ritual checklist; it describes a whole pattern of life.

questions.question: What are “sanctuary” and “holy hill” doing in the opening verse?
questions.answer: In the verse, they name the place associated with Yahweh’s presence: “your sanctuary” and “your holy hill.” many psalms are oriented toward Jerusalem and temple worship, but this chapter itself does not narrate a temple event. The terms set the question in worship language while the answer reaches into daily behavior.

questions.question: Does “A Psalm by David” settle who wrote it?
questions.answer: The heading reads, “A Psalm by David.” David is the dominant named figure in Psalms headings, but the Hebrew construction behind such headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging. Readers differ on how much historical authorship each Davidic heading establishes, so the safest statement here is that the received heading associates the psalm with David.

questions.question: What does “speaks truth in his heart” mean?
questions.answer: Verse 2 pairs doing what is right with speaking truth “in his heart.” In the psalm’s own wording, truthfulness is not only public speech; it reaches the inner person. The next verse then shows how truthfulness affects words spoken about other people.

questions.question: Why does the psalm care so much about speech?
questions.answer: Verse 3 names three refusals: not slandering with the tongue, not doing evil to a friend, and not casting slurs against a fellow man. The psalm treats speech as part of whether someone’s life fits the opening question about dwelling near Yahweh. It does not separate worship from how a person talks about neighbors.

questions.question: Is verse 4 telling readers to hate people?
questions.answer: Verse 4 says that a “vile man is despised” while “those who fear Yahweh” are honored. Readers differ on how to express this contrast responsibly: some emphasize moral discernment, while others stress the danger of turning poetic description into contempt for persons. What the verse clearly does is contrast what the righteous person refuses to admire with whom that person honors.

questions.question: What is hard about “keeps an oath even when it hurts”?
questions.answer: The phrase says the person does not change an oath simply because keeping it becomes costly. The verse does not discuss every possible conflict or abusive vow; it gives a concise portrait of reliability. Responsible readers should avoid using this line to demand harm while still hearing its plain stress on costly faithfulness.

questions.question: What are “usury” and “bribe” about in verse 5?
questions.answer: Verse 5 describes someone who does not lend money for usury and does not take a bribe against the innocent. The chapter’s concern is not abstract finance but exploitation and corrupted justice. The person welcomed in the psalm refuses to profit in ways that harm the vulnerable or distort a case against the innocent.

questions.question: What does “shall never be shaken” promise?
questions.answer: The closing line says, “He who does these things shall never be shaken.” Within the psalm, that assurance belongs to the person just described across verses 2–5. Psalms elsewhere includes suffering and lament, so this line should be read as this psalm’s wisdom assurance rather than a claim that faithful people never face trouble.

glossary.def: The holy place named in the opening question as Yahweh’s dwelling place.
The elevated holy place in verse 1 where the question imagines living near Yahweh.
Harmful speech named in verse 3 as something the described person does not do with his tongue.
A solemn promise in verse 4 that the righteous person keeps even when it hurts.
Lending practice named in verse 5 that the described person refuses.
A payment or advantage in verse 5 that would be taken against the innocent; the righteous person refuses it.
